reference.source: Braunwald's Heart Disease / infiltrative cardiomyopathy consensus documents
clinicalPearls: A leading cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy, with the two main forms being AL (light-chain) and ATTR (transthyretin) amyloidosis
ATTR includes a hereditary variant from TTR mutations and a wild-type form of older age, formerly termed senile amyloidosis
Classic clue is left ventricular wall thickening on echo with paradoxically low voltages on the ECG
Echocardiography often shows a granular sparkling myocardial texture and impaired longitudinal strain with apical sparing
Red-flag associations include carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, and biceps tendon rupture, especially in ATTR
Bone-avid scintigraphy strongly supports ATTR once a monoclonal protein has been excluded, sometimes avoiding biopsy
AL disease needs urgent haematology-directed treatment, while ATTR is managed with transthyretin stabilisers or gene-silencing therapy
reference.pathophysiology: Cardiac amyloidosis results from extracellular deposition of misfolded protein as insoluble amyloid fibrils within the myocardium. In AL amyloidosis the fibrils derive from immunoglobulin light chains produced by a clonal plasma cell disorder, whereas in ATTR they derive from transthyretin, either mutated in the hereditary form or wild-type in older patients. Progressive infiltration stiffens the ventricular walls, producing restrictive physiology with impaired diastolic filling, and disrupts conduction tissue; light chains additionally exert a direct cardiotoxic effect, contributing to the more rapid deterioration seen in AL disease.
additionalDifferentials: Other infiltrative or storage cardiomyopathies such as Fabry disease
Endomyocardial fibrosis and other restrictive cardiomyopathies
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography assessing wall thickness, diastolic function, and longitudinal strain with apical sparing
ECG demonstrating low voltages, pseudo-infarct pattern, and conduction disease
Serum free light chains, serum and urine immunofixation to identify a monoclonal protein
Bone-avid scintigraphy such as pyrophosphate imaging to detect ATTR uptake
Cardiac MRI showing diffuse late enhancement and abnormal T1 mapping, with tissue biopsy and typing when needed
redFlags: Rapidly progressive heart failure, particularly in AL disease
A newly identified monoclonal protein requiring urgent haematology assessment
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on subtype and stage; untreated AL cardiac amyloidosis has a particularly poor outlook, whereas earlier diagnosis and modern ATTR therapies can slow progression and improve survival.
pitfalls: Mistaking the wall thickening for hypertensive or hypertrophic disease and missing the diagnosis
Interpreting bone-avid scintigraphy as diagnostic of ATTR without excluding a monoclonal protein
Using standard heart-failure agents that provoke hypotension in restrictive physiology
Delaying haematology referral in suspected AL disease
management: Confirm and type the amyloid first, since treatment is subtype-specific: anti-plasma-cell therapy for AL and transthyretin stabilisers or silencers for ATTR
AL disease treated with plasma-cell-directed therapy such as bortezomib-based regimens with daratumumab to suppress the clonal light chains, alongside haematology
ATTR disease treated with a transthyretin stabiliser such as tafamidis or a gene-silencing agent such as patisiran or inotersen to slow progression
Heart failure managed with cautious diuresis, avoiding agents poorly tolerated in restrictive amyloid physiology such as beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers and digoxin
Management of conduction disease and arrhythmia, with pacing where indicated and anticoagulation for atrial arrhythmias
Surveillance with echocardiography, cardiac biomarkers and staging, and awareness of red-flag features such as carpal tunnel syndrome
Genetic counselling and family screening in hereditary ATTR, with cardiac or combined transplantation considered in selected patients
